client: I've been feeling really stretched thin lately, and honestly I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything. I'm in my second year of grad school and I'm also working part-time at a coffee shop to pay rent, and it feels like no matter how hard I try, I'm always falling short in both places. I keep lying awake at night thinking I'm going to fail my program or lose my job, and I don't know how much longer I can keep this up.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're exhausted — you're carrying a genuinely heavy load, and that feeling of always falling short despite working so hard sounds really demoralizing and isolating. I want to gently notice something you said: that you keep *thinking* you're going to fail — and I'm curious whether there's a difference between that fear feeling very real at 2am and what's actually happening in your program and at work. What does "falling short" actually look like day to day — are there specific moments or situations where that feeling hits the hardest?

client: Honestly, the hardest moments are when I'm at the coffee shop and I get an email from my advisor asking about my thesis progress, and I just freeze because I haven't made as much headway as I should have. Or when I'm finally sitting down to work on research and I'm so tired from my shift that I can't string two coherent thoughts together, and then I feel guilty for not pushing through anyway. I guess you're right that I'm not actually failing yet, but it doesn't feel that way — it feels like I'm one bad week away from everything falling apart.
therapist: That image of freezing when your advisor's email comes in — while you're standing in the middle of a coffee shop shift — really captures how impossible your situation feels, like you're being pulled in two directions with no space to breathe. It's worth noticing that "I haven't made as much progress as I *should* have" is doing a lot of work in your mind — that word "should" often carries a harsh, unforgiving standard that doesn't account for the very real constraints you're operating under. I'm wondering, if a close friend described your exact schedule and situation to you, would you judge their progress the same way you're judging yours?

client: I know what you're going for with that question, and honestly, no, I wouldn't judge a friend that harshly — I'd probably tell them they're doing amazing just for surviving that schedule. But it feels different when it's me, because I feel like I chose this situation, so I don't really deserve the same sympathy. Like, no one forced me to apply to grad school or take this job, so the pressure I'm under is kind of my own fault.
therapist: That insight — recognizing you'd be kinder to a friend — is actually really important, and it takes honesty to see it so clearly. But I want to gently push back on this idea that *choosing* something means you forfeit the right to struggle with it — people choose to have children, choose demanding careers, choose things they love, and still deserve compassion when those things are hard. I'm curious where that belief came from — that self-inflicted difficulty somehow doesn't count — because it sounds like it might be a rule you've been carrying for a long time, not just something that applies to grad school?

client: That question kind of stopped me because I think you might be right that it goes further back than grad school. Growing up, I got the message pretty clearly that complaining about things you brought on yourself was just whining, and that you should either fix it or stop talking about it. I'm not sure I ever really questioned that until just now, but I also don't know how you just... unlearn something that's been in your head for that long.
therapist: What you just did — pausing to question a belief you've carried since childhood — is actually the first and hardest step in unlearning it, so give yourself credit for that moment of real awareness. These deeply held rules don't disappear overnight, but they do loosen over time when we start noticing them in action, like catching yourself thinking "I don't deserve sympathy" and asking "wait, says who?" I'm wondering, now that you can see where that rule came from, does it feel like something a wise, caring adult deliberately taught you — or more like a message you absorbed from a difficult environment that was doing its best but maybe got this one wrong?

client: I think it was more absorbed than taught, like nobody sat me down and said "you don't deserve help," it was just... the atmosphere. My parents were dealing with a lot of their own stuff and I think showing struggle just wasn't something that got rewarded, so I stopped doing it. But I guess what I'm sitting with now is — even if I can intellectually see that the rule was flawed, I don't know how to make myself actually feel like I deserve compassion when I'm in the middle of a hard moment, because it still just feels like weakness.
therapist: That gap between *knowing* something intellectually and *feeling* it in your body in a hard moment is one of the most real and frustrating parts of this kind of work, and it makes complete sense given that this pattern was wired in through years of experience, not just one conversation. The good news is that feelings follow behavior over time — meaning we don't have to wait until you *feel* deserving of compassion to start practicing small acts of self-compassion, and gradually the feeling tends to catch up. I'm curious — in those moments when you're frozen, exhausted, or spiraling at 2am, what do you think the tiniest possible gesture of kindness toward yourself might look like, even if it feels undeserved at first?

client: I guess maybe something like... putting my phone down when I get that advisor email during a shift and telling myself it can wait an hour, instead of letting it ruin the rest of my time there. But even saying that out loud feels a little uncomfortable, like I'm giving myself permission to be irresponsible. I think part of me worries that if I start being gentler with myself, I'll lose whatever edge is keeping me going and everything really will fall apart.
therapist: That idea of putting the phone down for an hour is actually a really wise and concrete instinct, and I want to highlight that choosing *when* to respond to an email is responsible time management, not irresponsibility — your advisor doesn't need an answer mid-shift. The fear that self-compassion will make you fall apart is incredibly common, but it's worth examining the evidence: right now you're running on self-criticism and fear, and it's leaving you frozen, exhausted, and awake at 3am — so is that "edge" actually working as well as you think it is? What do you imagine might actually happen if you tried that one small experiment this week — letting the email wait — and it turned out okay?

client: I think if it actually turned out okay, it would be kind of unsettling in a way, because it would mean I've been putting myself through all this unnecessary stress for nothing. And that's almost harder to sit with than the stress itself, if that makes any sense. I guess I'm willing to try it, but I'm already anticipating that even if the email waits fine, my brain will find some reason why that one time doesn't count as real evidence.
therapist: What you just described — that it might be *harder* to find out the stress was unnecessary — is a profound and honest insight, and it makes complete sense because it would mean grieving a pattern that's cost you a lot. And you're already anticipating your mind's defense mechanism, that "one time doesn't count" move, which is actually you getting ahead of your own brain in a really sophisticated way. I'm wondering if we could agree that noticing that dismissal — catching yourself saying "it doesn't count" — could itself be part of the experiment, so the goal isn't just whether the email waits okay, but whether you can observe how your mind tries to protect the old story?

client: That reframe actually makes it feel a little more manageable, because it takes some pressure off needing the experiment to "prove" something and just makes it about paying attention. But I'll be honest, I'm a little skeptical of my own ability to catch myself in those moments — when I'm already anxious and spiraling, I'm not exactly in a great headspace for calm self-observation. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to make that noticing part easier, because right now it sounds good in theory but I can imagine myself being way too deep in the panic to step back.
therapist: That's a really practical and self-aware concern — trying to observe your thoughts while you're already mid-spiral is a bit like trying to read a book while someone's shouting at you, so it makes sense that it feels unreliable. One thing that can help is creating a tiny "anchor" in advance — something physical and automatic, like taking one slow breath or even just feeling your feet on the floor — that gives your nervous system a half-second pause before the spiral fully takes hold, so the noticing doesn't have to be calm or perfect, just slightly slower than the panic. I'm curious, is there anything you already do — even unconsciously — that sometimes gives you even a brief moment of steadiness when things feel overwhelming?

client: Actually, now that you mention it, there's this thing I do sometimes where I'll step outside the coffee shop for a minute between orders and just look at something across the street — like a tree or a building — and it does seem to slow things down a little, even if just for a second. I never really thought of it as something intentional, it was just something I drifted into doing. I guess I'm a little surprised that something I was already doing kind of fits what you're describing, though I'm not sure I can make it reliable enough to actually count on when things get really bad.
therapist: The fact that you already discovered this on your own — without anyone telling you to — actually says a lot about your own instincts for self-care, even when part of you insists you don't deserve it. What you're describing, that deliberate shift of attention to something external and neutral, is genuinely a grounding technique, and the beautiful thing is it doesn't need to be perfect or reliable 100% of the time to be worth leaning into more intentionally. I'm wondering what it might feel like to think of that doorway as your version of "putting the phone down" — a small, already-yours act of compassion that you could consciously choose next time, rather than waiting to see if you drift into it?

client: Framing it as "already mine" does make it feel less like homework and more like something I'm just... allowing myself to use on purpose, which is a little easier to accept. I think I can try that, though part of me is still waiting for the catch — like maybe it works for small stress but when I get an email from my advisor mid-rush and there are five people in line, stepping outside isn't exactly an option. I guess I'm wondering what I'm supposed to do when even that small exit isn't available to me.
therapist: That's a really fair and grounded concern — you're not just accepting the idea, you're stress-testing it against your real life, which is exactly the right instinct. When the physical exit isn't available, the same principle can sometimes work in a smaller, invisible way — even just briefly fixing your gaze on one specific object in the room for a few seconds, or feeling the counter under your hands, can offer a tiny version of that same pause without anyone around you noticing. I'm curious, when you imagine that moment — advisor email, five people in line, no way out — what would feel like even a 10% reduction in the spiral, rather than needing it to fully stop?
